aristotle.title: Aristotle of Stagira
aristotle.text: Born in 384 BC at Stagira in the north, son of Nicomachus, physician to the Macedonian king. He came to Athens at seventeen and stayed at the Academy for some twenty years. Ancient writers remembered him as slight, with small eyes, a lisp, rings on his fingers and carefully cut hair.

plato.title: Plato
plato.text: Athenian, pupil of Socrates, founder of the Academy around 387 BC. In 367 he is about sixty and about to sail for Syracuse, where Dionysius the Younger has invited him. He teaches by questions, in conversation, and writes dialogues rather than treatises.

speusippus.title: Speusippus
speusippus.text: Plato's nephew and, after Plato's death in 347, head of the Academy. Later writers called him quick-tempered. He set up statues of the Graces in the shrine of the Muses that Plato had founded.

xenocrates.title: Xenocrates of Chalcedon
xenocrates.text: Grave and slow of speech. Plato kept telling him to 'sacrifice to the Graces', and said that Xenocrates needed a spur and Aristotle a bridle. He would head the Academy from 339 BC, and was famous for being impossible to bribe.

eudoxus.title: Eudoxus of Cnidus
eudoxus.text: Mathematician and astronomer: the theory of proportion, the method of exhaustion, and a model of the heavens made of nested rotating spheres. As a poor young man he lodged at the Piraeus and walked to the Academy every day. (That he ran the school while Plato was in Syracuse is a modern guess, not an ancient report.)

diogenes.title: Diogenes of Sinope
diogenes.text: The Cynic, who lived in a storage jar and owned a cloak, a staff and a bag. He carried a lamp in daylight, 'looking for a human being'. Told that Plato had defined man as a featherless biped, he plucked a chicken and brought it in: 'Here is Plato's man.' Most stories about him are anecdotes, some surely invented in antiquity.

academy.title: The Academy
academy.text: A sacred grove of the hero Hekademos outside the Dipylon. Hipparchus walled it; Cimon brought water, running tracks and shady walks. It held a gymnasium, altars, a shrine of the Muses, and the sacred olives. Plato taught here, and in a small garden of his own nearby.

demosion_sema.title: The Demosion Sema
demosion_sema.text: The state cemetery along the road from the Dipylon to the Academy. The war dead of each year were buried together, their names listed on stone by tribe, and a leading citizen gave a funeral speech. Pericles' speech of 431 BC is the most famous: the city itself, he said, was their monument.

dexileos.title: The stele of Dexileos
dexileos.text: A family monument for a young cavalryman, killed near Corinth in 394 BC at about twenty. The relief shows him riding down a fallen enemy. Unusually, the inscription gives his birth year, as if to answer anyone who blamed the cavalry for politics: he was too young to have been involved.

torch_race.title: The torch race
torch_race.text: At festivals runners lit torches at the altar of Prometheus in the Academy and raced to the city. Speed was not enough: if the leader's torch went out, victory passed to the next runner with a flame, and if every torch went out, no one won.

geometry_rumour.title: The inscription that isn't there
geometry_rumour.sources: First attested in the 6th century AD (Elias, Philoponus)
geometry_rumour.text: 'Let no one ignorant of geometry enter.' Later writers claimed this stood over the door of the Academy, but no source from Plato's time mentions it. Mathematics mattered enormously here; the inscription is probably a legend.

moriai.title: The sacred olives
moriai.text: Olive trees belonging to Athena, said to descend from her gift to the city. They were protected by law; a speech by Lysias defends a man accused of removing the stump of one. Sophocles praises the grey-leaved olive of Colonus that no enemy could destroy.

mouseion.title: The shrine of the Muses
mouseion.text: Plato founded a shrine of the Muses in the Academy; Speusippus later added statues of the Graces. Pausanias also saw an altar of the Muses here. Its exact form and place are unknown; the game's shrine among cypresses is a reconstruction.

palaestra.title: The palaestra
palaestra.sources: Vitruvius 5.11; excavations of the square peristyle
palaestra.text: A courtyard of sand surrounded by porticoes, where young men wrestled, oiled and dusted. Vitruvius describes exedrae where philosophers sat and argued, and rooms for oil, dust, bathing and the punching bag. Athletes trained naked and scraped themselves clean with a strigil.

cimon.title: Cimon's water
cimon.text: In the 460s BC the general Cimon turned the Academy from a dry place into a watered grove, with clear running tracks and shady walks. The water came from the Cephissus. The layout of the channels in the game is invented.

lyceum.title: The Lyceum
lyceum.text: A public gymnasium in a sanctuary of Apollo Lykeios, east of the city by the Ilissos. Aristotle taught there from 335 BC. As a foreigner he could not own land; the school's garden, covered walk and shrine of the Muses are known from his successor Theophrastus' will.

sicily.title: Plato in Sicily
sicily.text: In 367 BC Dionysius I of Syracuse died. His brother-in-law Dion persuaded Plato to come and educate the young heir, Dionysius II. Plato went, he wrote later, partly so as not to seem a man of words only. Within months Dion was exiled and Plato was kept at court almost as a prisoner. He returned to Athens about 365.

eudoxus_pleasure.title: Eudoxus on pleasure
eudoxus_pleasure.text: Eudoxus argued that pleasure is the good, because all creatures, rational and irrational, aim at it. Aristotle says people were convinced more by Eudoxus' character than by the argument, since he was thought exceptionally temperate. Plato's reply, in the Philebus, is that a life of pleasure joined with wisdom is better than pleasure alone, so pleasure cannot be the good itself. The scene where Eudoxus teaches it to newcomers is invented.

laches.title: Plato's Laches
laches.text: Two Athenian generals, Laches and Nicias, try to say what courage is. 'Standing firm in the line' fails against the Scythians who fight by retreating; 'endurance of the soul' fails because foolish endurance is not admirable; 'knowledge of what is to be feared' turns out to be all of virtue at once. The dialogue ends without an answer.

theaetetus.title: Theaetetus
theaetetus.sources: Plato, Theaetetus 142a–b, 147d–148b; scholium to Euclid XIII; Suda
theaetetus.text: Athenian mathematician and friend of Plato, who made him the hero of a dialogue. He classified irrational lengths and, by the ancient tradition, first constructed the octahedron and icosahedron and proved there are only five regular solids. He died in 369 BC after the fighting at Corinth, of wounds and dysentery.

timaeus_elements.title: The elements of the Timaeus
timaeus_elements.text: In the Timaeus, the four elements are made of tiny regular solids built from two kinds of right triangles: fire of tetrahedra (sharp, mobile), air of octahedra, water of icosahedra (smooth, rolling), earth of cubes (stable). The fifth solid, the dodecahedron, the god used 'for the whole'. Plato calls the account 'a likely story'.

eudoxus_spheres.title: Eudoxus' homocentric spheres
eudoxus_spheres.sources: Aristotle, Metaphysics Λ.8 1073b17–32; Simplicius, On Aristotle's De Caelo; Schiaparelli (1877), Yavetz (1998)
eudoxus_spheres.text: Eudoxus explained the wandering of the planets with spheres nested around the Earth, each turning steadily: four per planet, three each for the Sun and Moon, one for the fixed stars, twenty-seven in all. Two inner spheres turning against each other on tilted axes trace a figure-eight (the hippopede); added to the steady motion along the zodiac, it produces the planet's retrograde loops. The model works well for Jupiter and Saturn but fails for Mars. Aristotle later raised the count to fifty-five.

delian_problem.title: The Delian problem
delian_problem.sources: Eratosthenes, in Eutocius on Archimedes; Plutarch, De E apud Delphos 386e, De genio Socratis 579b–d, Quaestiones convivales 8.2.1
delian_problem.text: To end a plague, the Delians were told to double Apollo's cubic altar. Doubling the edge gives eight times the volume. Hippocrates of Chios reduced the problem to finding two mean proportionals; Archytas, Menaechmus and Eudoxus solved it. Plutarch has Plato say the god was rebuking the Greeks for neglecting geometry, and also has him scold those who used instruments. Eutocius attributes a mechanical solution to Plato himself, almost certainly wrongly.

divided_line.title: The Divided Line
divided_line.text: A line cut into unequal parts, each cut again in the same ratio: images, visible things, mathematical objects, Forms; and the four states of mind that go with them, eikasia, pistis, dianoia, noesis. The two middle segments always come out equal, a fact Plato does not mention.

cave.title: The Allegory of the Cave
cave.text: Prisoners chained since childhood see only shadows of objects carried before a fire. One is freed, turned around, dragged up into the sunlight; first he can bear only shadows and reflections, then things, then the night sky, and at last the sun. Back in the cave, his eyes no longer used to the dark, the others laugh at him and would kill whoever tried to free them. Plato insists the philosopher must nevertheless go back down.

axiothea.title: Axiothea of Phlius
axiothea.text: One of two women known to have studied with Plato, the other being Lasthenia of Mantinea. After reading the Republic she came to Athens and, according to Dicaearchus, attended the Academy wearing men's clothes. Her friendship with the player is invented.

third_man.title: The Third Man
third_man.sources: Plato, Parmenides 132a–b; Aristotle, Metaphysics A.9 990b17, Sophistical Refutations 22 178b36
third_man.text: If many large things are large by sharing in one Form of Largeness, and Largeness itself is large, then the large things together with Largeness need a further Form, and so on without end. Plato raised the objection against himself in the Parmenides; Aristotle gave it the name 'the third man' and used it against the Forms.

aristotle_biology.title: Aristotle the biologist
aristotle_biology.sources: Aristotle, History of Animals, Parts of Animals, Generation of Animals
aristotle_biology.text: About a quarter of Aristotle's surviving works are about animals: some five hundred kinds, many observed himself, much of it on Lesbos in the 340s. He classified them by blood, by how they reproduce and by their parts, and insisted that even the humblest animal has something wonderful in it. His start on it at the Academy is the game's invention.

plato_death.title: The death of Plato
plato_death.text: Plato died in 348/7 BC in his eighty-first year; Hermippus says at a wedding feast. He was buried in the Academy, near where he taught. His nephew Speusippus succeeded him; Aristotle and Xenocrates left Athens for Assos.

wonder.title: Philosophy begins in wonder
wonder.text: Socrates tells the young Theaetetus that wonder is the feeling of the philosopher, and philosophy has no other beginning.

philosopher_kings.title: Philosopher-kings
philosopher_kings.text: Cities will have no rest from trouble until philosophers rule, or rulers truly become philosophers.

ladder_of_love.title: The ladder of love
ladder_of_love.text: Love leads from one beautiful body to beauty in all bodies, to beautiful souls, laws and knowledge, and finally to beauty itself, unchanging.

forms.title: The Forms
forms.text: Beyond the many beautiful things there is Beauty itself, which they share in: unchanging, known by thought rather than sight.

recollection.title: Learning as recollection
recollection.text: An untaught boy, questioned step by step, finds the square double a given square. Socrates argues he was not taught but recalled what he already knew.

incommensurable.title: Incommensurable lengths
incommensurable.text: The diagonal of a square cannot be measured by any unit that also measures its side exactly. Yet geometry can still construct it.

ratio.title: Ratios of magnitudes
ratio.sources: Euclid, Elements V (attributed to Eudoxus by a scholiast); Proclus
ratio.text: Two lengths that share no common measure can still stand in a ratio, and ratios can be compared: Eudoxus defined when two ratios are equal without ever needing a common unit. It rescued geometry from the crisis of the incommensurable.

pleasure_good.title: Is pleasure the good?
pleasure_good.sources: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics X.2; Plato, Philebus
pleasure_good.text: Eudoxus: everything seeks pleasure, so pleasure is the good. Plato: pleasure mixed with wisdom is better than pleasure alone, so pleasure is not the good itself.

aporia.title: Aporia
aporia.text: A state of puzzlement, of having no way through. Socrates' questions often end there. Meno compared him to a stingray that numbs whoever it touches. Plato treats aporia as the start of inquiry: you look for what you know you lack.

five_solids.title: Only five regular solids
five_solids.text: At least three faces meet at each corner, and their angles must add to less than 360°. Only 3, 4 or 5 triangles, 3 squares or 3 pentagons pass that test.

homocentric_spheres.title: Saving the appearances
homocentric_spheres.text: Explain the irregular motions of the heavens by combining perfectly regular circular motions.

mean_proportionals.title: Two mean proportionals
mean_proportionals.text: If a : x = x : y = y : 2a, then a cube on x has twice the volume of a cube on a.

divided_line.title: Four kinds of seeing
divided_line.text: Images, things, mathematical objects, Forms: each grasped more clearly than the one below.

cave.title: Out of the cave
cave.text: Education is not putting sight into blind eyes but turning the whole soul around toward the light.

women_guardians.title: Women as guardians
women_guardians.text: No pursuit of the city belongs to a woman as a woman or to a man as a man: natures are distributed alike, and women may be guardians too.

third_man.title: The Third Man
third_man.text: If the Form shares the quality it explains, another Form is needed over both: an endless regress.

form_in_matter.title: Form in matter
form_in_matter.text: The form of a thing is in the thing, not apart from it: what makes a heron a heron is in the heron.
